title: The Submarine Cables Carrying 99% of Internet Traffic — Engineering Cheat Sheet
subtitle: The physical backbone of global digital infrastructure and low-latency networking.
summary: Submarine fiber optic cables represent the physical OSI Layer 1 of the global internet, moving nearly all international data traffic. Understanding this infrastructure is critical for engineers designing high-availability systems, CDN distribution, and global latency-sensitive distributed architectures.

key_concepts.name: DWDM (Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing)
key_concepts.detail: Optical multiplexing technique increasing bandwidth by combining multiple data signals onto a single fiber using different laser wavelengths, currently enabling terabit-per-second capacities across transoceanic distances.

key_concepts.name: Optical Amplification (EDFA)
key_concepts.detail: Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifiers placed at specific intervals along cables to boost signal strength without electrical conversion, mitigating signal attenuation caused by long-distance photon absorption in glass.

key_concepts.name: Submarine Cable Landing Stations (CLS)
key_concepts.detail: The critical interface points where undersea cable systems connect to terrestrial fiber backbones, serving as high-security hubs for power feed equipment and signal regeneration nodes.

code_cheatsheet.explanation: Uses ICMP to visualize the multi-hop path and identify latency spikes that may indicate intercontinental transit over specific cable systems.

code_cheatsheet.code: latency = ping_latency_ms(region_a, region_b) # Approx 130-150ms NYC to London
code_cheatsheet.explanation: Used in calculating RTT budgets for distributed database consensus protocols like Paxos or Raft that are limited by physical speed-of-light constraints.

best_practices: Design for multi-homing by utilizing diverse landing stations to prevent total regional isolation during cable cuts.
Implement asynchronous replication for cross-continental data stores to handle unavoidable RTT latency.
Utilize Anycast networking for edge delivery to route users to the nearest physical cable ingress point.
Monitor global outage maps via Submarine Cable Map APIs to anticipate regional packet loss patterns.

interview_qa.question: How do submarine cables impact the design of a globally distributed database?
interview_qa.answer: Latency is bounded by the speed of light in fiber (~200,000 km/s), making synchronous cross-continental writes prohibitively slow. Architects must prioritize eventual consistency or regional sharding to maintain performance.
